blocks.text: It is proved that פתן pethen is the asp.

Another name of the asp is פתן pethen. For so most render this word. And that this rendering is correct is suggested by several passages on the poison of the פתן pethen ^{*)}. [col. 381] Thus Job XX, 14. מרורת פתנים בקרבו. Here the Elders have Χολὴ ἀσπίδος ἐν γαστρὶ αὐτοῦ [cholē aspidos en gastri autou], and the Vulgate translator The gall of asps within. And a little later, in verse sixteen, ראש פתנים יינק. Here the Elders have Θυμὸν δὲ δρακόντων θηλάσειεν [thymon de drakontōn thēlaseien]. But other Greek translators have Χολὴν ἀσπίδων μυζήσει [cholēn aspidōn myzēsei], and Jerome He shall suck the head of asps. Again Deut. XXXII, 33. וראש פתנים אכזר, And the cruel poison of pethanim. For this the Greek has Καὶ θυμὸς ἀσπίδων ἀνίατος [kai thymos aspidōn aniatos]; whence the Vulgate translator has And the incurable poison of asps. As if for אכזר they had read אין זר, there is no cure. For זר means to treat a wound, Esa. I, 6, and מזור the treatment of a wound, Ier. XXX, 13. The asp's poison is, of course, the sharpest of all, and penetrates the vital organs very swiftly. Aelian's words, book 9, ch. 61, are: Ὀξύτατόν ἐστι τὸ ἐξ αὐτῆς φάρμακον, καὶ διαδραμεῖν ὤκιστον [oxytaton esti to ex autēs pharmakon, kai diadramein ōkiston]. Hence the common proverb in Apostolius and Erasmus, Δῆγμα ἀσπίδος [dēgma aspidos], The bite of an asp, for an incurable wound; because one who has been bitten by an asp is rarely healed. This is attested by writers not to be despised. Aristotle, book 8 of the History, ch. 29: Τὰ δὲ τῶν ὄφεων δήγματα πολὺ διαφέρουσιν. ἥτε γὰρ ἀσπὶς ἐν Λιβύῃ γίνεται, ἐξ οὗ ὄφεως ποιοῦσι τὸ σηπτικόν· καὶ ἄλλως ἀνιάτως [ta de tōn opheōn dēgmata poly diapherousin. hēte gar aspis en Libyē ginetai, ex hou opheōs poiousi to sēptikon; kai allōs aniatōs]. The bites of serpents differ greatly. For the asp is born in Africa, [III, 157] from which they make a putrefying ointment; and besides, incurably—supply it bites. Pliny, book 8, ch. 23: That the necks of asps swell (it is commonly known), and there is no remedy for their stroke, except if the parts touched are immediately amputated. Aelian, book 1, ch. 54: Ἀσπίδος δὲ ἀκούω μόνον δῆγμα ἀνίατον εἶναι, καὶ ἐπικουρίας κρεῖττον [aspidos de akouō monon dēgma aniaton einai, kai epikourias kreitton]; I hear that the bite of the asp alone is incurable and stronger than every remedy. And book 6, ch. 38: Τῶν ὑπ’ ἀσπίδος δηχθέντων οὐ μνημονεύεται οὐδεὶς ἐξάντης γεγονέναι τοῦ κακοῦ. Ἔνθεν τοι καὶ τοὺς βασιλεῖς ἀκούω τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ἐπὶ τῶν διαδημάτων φορεῖν πεποικιλμένας ἀσπίδας, τῆς ἀρχῆς αἰνιττομένους τὸ ἀνίκητον [tōn hyp’ aspidos dēchthentōn ou mnēmoneuetai oudeis exantēs gegonenai tou kakou. enthen toi kai tous basileis akouō tōn Aigyptiōn epi tōn diadēmatōn phorein pepoikilmenas aspidas, tēs archēs ainittomenous to anikēton]. Of those bitten by an asp, none is recorded to have escaped the evil (that is, death). This is why, I hear, the kings of Egypt wear asps depicted on their diadems, to signify thereby the invincible strength of their rule. And further below: Οἱ δηχθέντες ὑπ’ ἀσπίδων οὐ περαιτέρω βιοῦσι τετάρτης ὥρας [hoi dēchthentes hyp’ aspidōn ou peraiterō biousi tetartēs hōras]; Those bitten by asps do not live beyond the fourth hour. Philes, ch. 59:

Τῆς ἀσπίδος τὸ δῆγμα δῆγμ’ ἔστι θανάτου. Μὴ, μὴ, Γαληνὲ, μηδὲ φάρμακον χέῃς. [tēs aspidos to dēgma dēgm’ esti thanatou. mē, mē, Galēne, mēde pharmakon cheēs.] The bite of the asp brings sudden death. Do not, do not, Galen, pour in a drug.

He addresses Galen in vain, since this is amply confirmed by the testimony of Galen himself, book 1 On Theriac, chapter 8, where he says this of asps: Πολλάκις ἐθεασάμην ἐγὼ ἐν τῇ μεγάλῃ Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τὸ τάχος τοῦ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γιγνομένου θανάτου. ὅταν γάρ τινα, τούτῳ τῷ νόμῳ τῆς κολάσεως κατακριθέντα, φιλανθρώπως καὶ ταχέως ἀποκτεῖναι θέλωσι, προσβάλλοντες αὐτοῦ τοῖς στέρνοις τὸ θηρίον, καὶ ποιήσαντες ὀλίγον περιπατῆσαι, οὕτω ταχέως ἀναιροῦσι τὸν ἄνθρωπον [pollakis etheasamēn egō en tē megalē Alexandreia to tachos tou hyp’ autou gignomenou thanatou. hotan gar tina, toutō tō nomō tēs kolaseōs katakrithenta, philanthrōpōs kai tacheōs apokteinai thelōsi, prosballontes autou tois sternois to thērion, kai poiēsantes oligon peripatēsai, houtō tacheōs anairousi ton anthrōpon]. In the great city of Alexandria I often saw how swiftly they bring death. For whenever they wish to kill humanely and quickly someone condemned under the law of this punishment, they put the beast to his breast and make it walk about a little, and in this way they kill the man at once. Therefore treading on asps is extremely dangerous. And the Psalmist, to signify that a good man is preserved by God even among the most bitter enemies, says that he will tread on asps and dragons unharmed, Psal. XCI, 13. Similar is the saying of the ancient interpreters of dreams in the Suda:
Ὄφεις πατεῖν, τὰ κέντρα τῶν ἐχθρῶν λύει· [opheis patein, ta kentra tōn echthrōn lyei] He who treads on snakes escapes the assault of enemies.
